string.text: This is a standard .45 ACP (11.43x23mm) cartridge used in the Colt M1911, SIG Sauer P220, HK USP Compact, and Desert Eagle .45 pistols. Renowned for its high accuracy and lethality, it has remained popular for over a century. A drawback of this caliber is its low muzzle velocity, which results from the heavy weight of the bullet combined with a relatively modest propellant charge.

This .45 ACP (11.43x23mm) cartridge features a lead expanding bullet known as Hydra-Shok that offers excellent stopping power and penetration. This is an enhanced-performance round designed for use with the Colt M1911, SIG Sauer P220, HK USP Compact, and Desert Eagle .45 pistols.
Standard 12-gauge round filled with 6mm shot. Highly lethal at close range. Only suitable for the TOZ-34, TOZ BM-16, Mossberg Maverick 88, and Franchi SPAS-12 shotguns.

A specialized 12-gauge round that's similiar to a slug, but more pointed. Its fins add stability, resulting in increased accuracy. The massive steel body of the bullet can penetrate any body armor. Only suitable for the TOZ-34, TOZ BM-16, Mossberg Maverick 88, and Franchi SPAS-12 shotguns.

This heavy 12-gauge slug round is normally used for hunting big game, but is also good for other purposes. Instead of piercing, this hefty slug simply crushes through armor. Only suitable for the TOZ-34, TOZ BM-16, Mossberg Maverick 88, and Franchi SPAS-12 shotguns.

An armor-piercing 5.45x39mm caliber cartridge for the AKS-74, AKS-74U, and RPK-74 assault rifles. \nDeveloped in the mid-1990s, when even an upgraded FMJ round proved insufficient to reliably penetrate modern military body armor.

Standard 5.45x39mm caliber cartridge for the AKS-74, AKS-74U, and RPK-74 assault rifles. \nDeveloped to replace the 7.62x39mm caliber, this cartridge offers greater accuracy due to reduced recoil and an increased firing range.

An armor-piercing 5.56x45mm caliber cartridge for the Enfield L85, ZM LR-300, SIG SG 550, HK G36 and FN F2000 assault rifles. \nIt was developed based on the late 20th century military conflicts experience, which demonstrated that existing 5.56mm-caliber cartridges were not sufficient against armored combatants.

A standard issue NATO 5.56x45mm caliber cartridge for the Enfield L85, ZM LR-300, SIG SG 550, HK G36 and FN F2000 assault rifles. \nIt was specially designed for accurate automatic fire, and is widely known under its Belgian SS109 designation. It's currently produced in many countries around the world, for both military and civilian use.

A standard 5.7mm caliber cartridge for the FN P90 submachine gun. \nIts composite core, which consists of steel (in the front) and aluminum (in the rear), increases the cartridge's penetration capability, making it more effective against lightly armored targets.
A 5.7mm armor-piercing cartridge for the FN P90 submachine gun. \nThe cartridge features a lead core and an enhanced propellant charge, making it effective against moderately armored targets.

A model 1943 intermediate full-metal-jacket 7.62x39mm caliber cartridge for the AKMS and RPK assault rifles. \nDue to a long storage period, these rounds have significantly deteriorated, which leads to increased wear on the firearm.

An inexpensive-to-manufacture 7.62x54R caliber cartridge for the SVD and OTs-03 SVU sniper rifles. \nOne of the oldest military cartridges (adopted for service in 1891), still in widespread use in many Warsaw Pact countries.

A 7.62x54R 7N14 caliber cartridge for the SVD and OTs-03 SVU sniper rifles enhanced with elements of a gravitational artifact; manufactured by Cobalt. The cartridge’s lethality is significantly increased, though its use takes a heavy toll on the condition of the weapon.

A sniper armor-piercing (SAP) 7.62x54R cartridge for the SVD and OTs-03 SVU sniper rifles. \nA modern variant of the 7.62R cartridge, developed in the mid-1980s to engage armored targets without compromising firing accuracy. Due to a difficult economic situation, it was not adopted for service until 1999.

An armor-piercing 7.62x54R cartridge for SVD and OTs-03 SVU sniper rifles. \nA modern variant of the 7.62R cartridge, developed in the mid-1990s for engaging heavily armored targets. During its development, particular emphasis was placed on armor penetration, which had an impact on the ammunition's firing accuracy.

Standard 9x18mm caliber cartridge for the PM, PB, Fort-12, and APS pistols, as well as the AEK-919K submachine gun. \nAn inexpensive Soviet cartridge with weak armor-piercing capability, developed in the mid-1940s for use in new military pistols with a blowback action.

An armor-piercing 9x18mm caliber cartridge for the PM, PB, Fort-12, and APS pistols, as well as the AEK-919K submachine gun. \nA powerful cartridge featuring an expanding bullet with an armor-piercing core, developed in the late 1990s at the Tula Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) to enhance the combat effectiveness of standard-issue 9x18mm caliber weapons.

A 9x18mm caliber cartridge with enhanced ballistic characteristics, designed for the PM, PB, Fort-12, and APS pistols, as well as the AEK-919K submachine gun. \nDeveloped in the early 1990s as part of the "Grach" weapons design competition. \nDue to an increased propellant charge and a more pronounced armor-piercing effect, it is significantly more effective than the standard PM cartridge.

A standard 9x19mm caliber cartridge for the Browning HP-SA, Walther P99, Beretta 92FS, and GSh-18 pistols, as well as the HK MP5 submachine gun. \nDeveloped in 1902, it is currently the most widely used pistol ammunition in the world. The name "Parabellum" is derived from the telegraphic address of the Berlin-based arms manufacturer DWM, which alludes to the Latin adage "Si vis pacem, para bellum" ("If you want peace, prepare for war").

Improved 9x19mm cartridge with an expanding bullet and an armor-piercing core, designed for the Browning HP-SA, Walther P99, Beretta 92FS, and GSh-18 pistols, as well as the HK MP5 submachine gun. \nIt was developed by the Tula Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) in the early 1990s as part of the "Grach" competition for a new military sidearm. For their new GSh-18 pistol, the designers opted to make the bullet as light as possible while increasing its muzzle velocity.

An armor-piercing 9x39mm caliber cartridge designed for the OTs-12 "Tiss," OTs-14 "Groza," AS "Val," and VSS "Vintorez" firearms. Although it travels at a subsonic velocity, its specially designed bullet allows it to penetrate most types of body armor at ranges of up to 400 meters.

An inexpensive variant of the 9x39mm armor-piercing cartridge, designed for the OTs-12 "Tiss," OTs-14 "Groza," AS "Val," and VSS "Vintorez" firearms. Although it travels at a subsonic velocity, its specially designed bullet allows it to penetrate most types of body armor at ranges of up to 300 meters.

A 9x39mm caliber sniper cartridge designed for the OTs-12 "Tiss," OTs-14 "Groza," AS "Val," and VSS "Vintorez" firearms. It features a subsonic muzzle velocity, yet its heavy, specially designed bullet allows it to penetrate most types of body armor at ranges of up to 400 meters.

An energy-based magazine containing 2mm ferromagnetic projectiles, designed for a Gauss rifle. \nIt is not known for certain where or by whom it is manufactured, but the process clearly involves high-tech equipment and the harnessing of artifact energy.

An American-made, high-precision fragmentation grenade designed for the M203 under-barrel grenade launcher and the integrated grenade launcher of the FN F2000. \nThe HE (high-explosive) variant produces several hundred fragments upon detonation and is intended for the effective engagement of enemy infantry.
The OG-7B is a high explosive, tandem charge warhead grenade that's for the RPG-7V. It's devastating against mutants, stalkers, troops, and lightly armored vehicles.

A frag grenade for the GP-25 "Kostyor" under-barrel grenade launcher, the integrated grenade launcher of the OTs-14 "Groza," and the RG-6 revolving grenade launcher. \nThe casing features pre-cut rifling grooves, which impart a rotational motion to the grenade as it travels along the barrel bore.

The VOG-25P "bounding" frag grenade (nicknamed "Podkidysh" — "the one that pops up") is designed for use with the GP-25 "Kostyor" under-barrel grenade launcher, the integrated grenade launcher of the OTs-14 "Groza," and the RG-6 revolving grenade launcher. \nUpon striking an obstacle, it leaps upward and detonates in the air at a height of approximately 1.5 meters, which enhances its lethality.
A flashlight that has a modified bulb and voltage regulator, giving it better brightness. Quite useful at nighttime or in areas with little or no lighting

This specific G36 has been altered by spraying powder from a grounded up gravitational artifact onto the barrel, improving overall accuracy.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.,
M209 grenade

A defensive hand grenade F-1 , enhanced by the energy of a gravitational artifact. \nThe blast radius and explosive power are significantly increased; it is recommended to throw it from a considerable distance.

A defensive hand grenade with a large shrapnel-effect radius. It is recommended to throw it only from behind cover. \nIt was developed by Soviet designers in the late 1930s based on the French F-1 defensive grenade from the First World War.
An RGD-5 offensive hand grenade, enhanced by the energy of a gravitational artifact. \nThe blast radius and explosive power are significantly increased; use with caution.

An offensive hand grenade that is technologically advanced, safe to handle, and inexpensive to mass-produce. \nIts shrapnel-effect radius is small, allowing it to be used during an assault without the risk of harming one's own troops who are positioned behind cover.

A Russian-made single-shot 40mm under-barrel grenade launcher designed for weapons used by Warsaw Pact countries. This specific variant is equipped with special mounts for attachment to the AKMS assault rifle. 
 Ammunition:
 VOG-25 grenade,
 VOG-25P grenade.

A Russian-made single-shot 40mm under-barrel grenade launcher for the AKS-74 assault rifle. 
 Ammunition:
 VOG-25 grenade,
 VOG-25P grenade.
An American-made single-shot 40mm under-barrel grenade launcher for the Enfield L85, HK G36, ZM LR-300, and SIG SG 550 assault rifles.\n Ammunition:\n M406 HE grenade.
An old, Soviet-made optical sight with 2.8x magnification. \nIncludes an adapter with a "dovetail" mount, designed for attachment to the AKMS assault rifle.

A widely used Soviet-made 4x optical sight designed for weapons with a "dovetail" mounting rail, including the AKS-74 and AS "Val" assault rifles, the RPK and RPK-74 light machine guns, and the OTs-14 "Groza" assault rifle-grenade launcher system.
A 4x optical weapon sight, manufactured in NATO countries and featuring a Picatinny rail mount; designed for use with assault rifles such as the ZM LR-300 and SIG SG 550.
A modern suppressor with a set of adapters for firearms of any caliber. \nIt significantly reduces the volume of gunshots, but has a negative impact on the weapon's ballistics.

The AEK-919K "Kashtan" submachine gun was developed at the Kovrov Mechanical Plant in the mid-1990s. The design was initially based on the Austrian Steyr MPi-69; however, after a small trial batch was produced, a number of flaws were identified, necessitating further refinement. 
The updated model was designated the AEK-919K and was intended for use by law enforcement special units and combat vehicle crews. It is equipped with an integrated suppressor.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x18mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

The AK-74 series is a direct descendant of the AK and AKM assault rifles. Following the global trend toward small-caliber, low-impulse ammunition and the weapons designed for it, the designers adapted the already proven and battle-tested platform to the new 5.45mm caliber. 
Compared to its Western counterparts, the AK-74 offers slightly lower accuracy and precision, but compensates with high reliability, ease of use, and ruggedness. 
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.45x39mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 5.45x39mm AP.

A variant of the AK-74 with an integrated higher-magnification sight, developed for the USSR Ministry of Defense competition aimed at creating an assault rifle with significantly improved accuracy and shot-grouping performance. Although the competition was won by the Nikonov designed assault rifle, small batches of the AKS-74 “Yenisei” continue to be produced on the account of special orders.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.45x39mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 5.45x39mm AP.

The merits of the Kalashnikov assault rifle are well known: exceptional reliability, ruggedness, ease of use and maintenance, and low cost. Its drawbacks, however, are equally well known: poor ergonomics, rather crude sights, significant recoil, and low accuracy. 
When the AKM was developed, the operational experience gained with the original rifle was partially taken into account; it became lighter and even more reliable, and the addition of a muzzle compensator helped reduce recoil, though the designers were unable to fully resolve all the issues. 
The AKMS variant is distinguished by its folding metal stock.
 Ammunition:
 standard 7.62x39mm.

The AKS-74U short-barreled assault rifle was developed in the late 1970s, based on the AKS-74, specifically for combat vehicle crews, artillery gun crews, and other military personnel for whom a standard-issue assault rifle would be too bulky. 
In terms of size and weight, it is comparable to a submachine gun; however, the type of ammunition it uses classifies it as an assault rifle. 
Its compactness and the high penetrating power of its rounds are its primary advantages, while its drawbacks include a limited effective range and a tendency to overheat during sustained automatic fire.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.45x39mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 5.45x39mm AP.

A variant of the AKS-74U featuring an integral suppressor, designed for special operations forces. Due to a number of design flaws, a search for a replacement began shortly after it entered service. 
The “Pikhta” and “Tiss” projects aimed to modernize the AKS-74UB; however, despite significant improvements, they failed to outperform alternatives such as the AS “Val”. Nevertheless, it continues to be produced in small batches on a special-order basis.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.45x39mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 5.45x39mm AP.

At first glance this looks like the legendary AKMSU, but turns out it is a work of an unknown, amateur gunsmith who cobbled it together using parts from an AKMS, an AKS-74U, and an OTs-14 “Groza”. One can only guess who created this "Frankenstein" and for what purpose. \n Ammunition:\n standard 7.62x39mm.

The Stechkin APS was adopted for service in 1951 as a personal self-defense weapon for officers, combat vehicle crews, and other categories of military personnel who, according to their official designation, were not issued larger, bulkier weapons. 
In the 1990s, it was effectively employed by Russian law enforcement agencies as a submachine gun equivalent, thanks to its high firepower and large magazine capacity.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x18mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

One of the most popular pistols of the late 20th century, developed by the Italian firm Fabbrica d'Armi Pietro Beretta. It gained significant prominence after winning the 1985 competition for a new sidearm for the U.S. Armed Forces. Upon its adoption, the model 92F, which was the version entered into the competition, underwent substantial modifications and was redesignated as the 92FS. 
It is favored by military and law enforcement agencies worldwide, as well as by members of the criminal underworld, who value its high-capacity magazine and common caliber.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x19 mm FMJ,
 improved 9x19 mm JHP.

The primary feature that distinguishes this rare model from the widely used 92 series is its three-round burst firing mode, as well as a higher RPM, an enlarged 21-round magazine, and a heavier slide. 
It was taken out of production in 1993 following the emergence of more affordable submachine guns, such as the MP5. How such a rare specimen ended up in the Zone remains unknown. 
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x19mm Parabellum,
 improved 9x19mm JSP-AP.

A classic Soviet side-by-side shotgun, manufactured by the Tula Arms Plant (TOZ) between 1957 and 1969. During this period, approximately 3 million BM-16s were produced, many of which have survived to the present day. Moreover, despite the high production volume, there was often a waiting list for these shotguns in the Siberian taiga.
 Ammunition:
 12x70Buckshot,
 12x76mm Slug,
 12x76mm Dart.

The BM-16 shotgun belonging to the legendary Dark Stalker looks no different from the standard model, except for its remarkably light weight.
 Ammunition:
 12x70Buckshot,
 12x76mm Slug,
 12x76mm Dart.

The classic Colt M1911, designed by J. M. Browning in the early 20th century, was adopted by the U.S. Armed Forces in 1911. After more than 70 years of faithful service to the military, it was replaced by the Italian-made Beretta 92FS; yet, to this day, it remains one of the most popular pistols in the United States. 
It is a reliable, heavy handgun, whose limited magazine capacity is partially offset by the power of its cartridge.
 Ammunition:
 standard .45 ACP,
 improved .45 ACP Hydra-Shok.

A .45 ACP variant of the Desert Eagle, developed as an effective response to the mutated monstrosities of the Zone. 
A true weapon for true heroes — big, heavy, and devastatingly lethal.
 Ammunition:
 standard .45 ACP,
 improved .45 ACP Hydra-Shok.

The F2000 modular assault rifle and grenade launcher system, manufactured by the Belgian firm FN Herstal, features an integrated, adjustable 4x magnification sight and a 40mm grenade launcher. 
The design’s standout innovation is its unique forward-ejection system for spent casings; this makes the weapon equally convenient for both left- and right-handed users and resolves a major drawback of the "bullpup" configuration — the tendency for ejected casings to strike the shooter in the face when firing from the left shoulder.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.,
M209 grenade

A Ukrainian police-issue pistol designed to replace the Soviet-era Makarov pistols, which have become both obsolete and physically worn out. 
Compared to the Makarov (PM), the Fort-12 offers advantages such as a 12-round magazine, an ergonomic grip, and greater shooting accuracy; however, its drawbacks include lower reliability and a heavier weight.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x18mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

An assault rifle manufactured by the German firm Heckler & Koch, developed in the early 1990s. It features a built-in, adjustable 3x optic and a folding polymer stock. 
The G36 is a prime example of a modern weapon — lightweight, reliable, and ergonomic.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

A mysterious weapon that operates on the principle of a Gauss cannon. Its manufacturer is not definitively known, but since it uses the energy of artifacts to fire, it can be assumed that the weapon is produced within the Zone. 
It is an ultra-precise, silent, and extremely powerful weapon, with its only drawback being a low rate of fire. 
 Ammunition:
 2mm gauss rounds.

A mysterious weapon that operates on the principle of a Gauss cannon. Its manufacturer is not definitively known, but since it uses the energy of artifacts to fire, it can be assumed that the weapon is produced within the Zone. 
It is an ultra-precise, silent, and extremely powerful weapon, with its only drawback being a low rate of fire. 
This model uses an extended 15-round magazine. 
 Ammunition:
 2mm gauss rounds.

A compact assault rifle and grenade launcher system featuring a bullpup configuration, developed by the Tula Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) based on the OTs-12 "Tiss." 
The "Groza" design shares 70 percent of its components with Kalashnikov-pattern assault rifles and is characterized by high reliability. Its advantages also include the use of a powerful subsonic cartridge and a high versatility, provided by an integrated grenade launcher.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x39mm PAB-9,
 armor-piercing 9x39mm SP-6,
 sniper 9x39mm SP-5,
under-barrel launcher - VOG-25 and VOG-25P grenades.

A variant of the OTs-14 “Groza” weapon system chambered for 7.62mm, developed for needs of Russian spetsnaz. The primary advantage of this modification is the ability to use standard 30-round magazines from Kalashnikov-pattern rifles, which simplifies logistics and ammunition standardization.
 
Ammunition:
standard 7.62x39mm
under-barrel launcher - VOG-25 and VOG-25P grenades.

The GSh-18 pistol was developed in the late 1990s at the Tula Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) under the leadership of renowned designers of aircraft cannons. It was adopted for service by the Russian Armed Forces in 2003. 
The advantages of the GSh-18 include its low weight, magazine capacity, good firing accuracy, and ergonomics. 
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x19mm Parabellum,
 improved 9x19mm JSP-AP.

The HK 53 is a carbine variant of the HK 33KA3 with a shortened barrel that's 221 millimeters long, a extended flash supressor and forend that's similar to HK MP5. No underbarrel grenade launcher or bayonet knife can be installed. This weapon has been manufactured since 1975 and is mainly used by special forces.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

The Browning High Power family of pistols is based on a barrel-locking mechanism developed by J. M. Browning in 1926 and has been manufactured by the Belgian firm FN Herstal since 1935. The pistol proved highly effective throughout the 20th century and remains in service in more than 100 countries today. 
A distinctive feature of the Hi-Power Single-Action variant is an automatic firing pin safety, which locks the firing pin in place until the trigger is fully pulled.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x19mm Parabellum,
 improved 9x19mm JSP-AP.
A knife enhanced by the energy of a gravi-artifact, crafted by Cobalt. Features significantly increased stabbing power.

A standard military bayonet designed for attachment to weapons used by Warsaw Pact countries. \nThough it has proven rather ineffective as a bayonet within the Zone, it has become a common item in the everyday gear of stalkers.

An old, rusty army bayonet. \nIt is fit for little more than opening tin cans, though even that is highly discouraged, given the risk of poisoning and the fact that it would leave the food tasting of rust.

The lack of markings and the inability to attach it to a firearm reveal it to be a poor imitation of the American M9 bayonet. Nevertheless, its distinctive Bowie-style blade makes it a reasonably decent edged weapon. \nNew batches occasionally appear among traders, and, thanks to their low price, they are quickly snapped up by stalkers.
The personal knife from a stalker named 'Scrap'. The handle is badly worn, but if you hold it, you'll notice that it fits perfectly in your hand.

A British assault rifle manufactured by RSAF Enfield, featuring an integrated 3x-magnification sight and developed in the late 1970s. 
Shortly after its adoption, numerous flaws were identified: an unreliable ammunition feed mechanism; poor corrosion resistance; low structural integrity in certain components; the center of gravity being shifted too far to the rear, causing the barrel to climb excessively during automatic fire. 
Following a failed modification program, the L85 was replaced by the German HK G36, and large numbers of the decommissioned rifles subsequently surfaced on the black market.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

A powerful and compact new-generation assault rifle, developed at the turn of the 21st century by the American firm Z-M Weapons based on the AR-15 platform. "LR-300" stands for "Light Rifle, effective at ranges up to 300 meters." 
In essence, all modifications were confined to the upper receiver, which helped reduce recoil and increase the rate of fire; furthermore, the use of a shortened bolt carrier allowed for the inclusion of a side-folding stock. 
It is highly impractical and requires meticulous maintenance, which is not always feasible in the Zone environment. 
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

A semi-automatic rifle developed by Para-Ordnance based on the ZM LR-300. Features an integrated higher-magnification sight. 
Modifications to the rifle's layout, along with refinements to its design and operating mechanism, significantly reduced its weight and improved its accuracy; however, these enhancements came at the cost of a smaller magazine capacity and the loss of automatic fire mode.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

The MP5 submachine gun was developed by the German firm Heckler & Koch in the 1960s; in terms of design, it is essentially a scaled-down version of the HK G3 rifle, chambered for a pistol cartridge. It was adopted by the West German police in 1966, and by the late 1970s, it had become standard-issue equipment for military and police special forces in a number of countries around the world. 
The success of the MP5 is due not only to the company’s astute marketing strategy but also to such merits as its reliability, ease of handling, and high firing accuracy.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x19mm Parabellum,
 improved 9x19mm JSP-AP.

Due to lower propellant gas pressure, the standard 9x18mm PM cartridge is incompatible with the bolt design of the MP5. This, it seems, is what prompted the technician working on this weapon to adapt it to fire the more powerful JSP-AP and +P+ cartridges instead. A small inscription can be seen on the stock: “Golmar”.
 Ammunition: 
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

A bullpup-configured submachine gun developed by the Belgian firm FN Herstal as a personal defense weapon for military personnel who, by the terms of their assignment, are not issued full-sized firearms. 
The P90 utilizes a specialized caliber capable of penetrating light body armor at ranges of up to 200 meters; it also features an extremely high rate of fire (approximately 1,000 rounds per minute), low recoil, and a high-capacity 50-round magazine. 
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

The silent pistol (PB) was developed based on the Makarov pistol for use by army reconnaissance units and KGB personnel; it was adopted for service in 1967. Features an integrated suppressor. 
Although technically obsolete, it remains quite effective in skilled hands.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x18mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

The Makarov pistol was adopted for service in 1951 as a self-defense weapon for officers. Although it was considered obsolete as early as the beginning of the 1990s, it remains in service in many post-Soviet countries. 
It is a compact and exceptionally reliable pistol that is simple to use and maintain, yet it possesses the drawbacks typical for its class: limited range and accuracy, and relatively low bullet effectiveness.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x18mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

In the early 1990s, the Makarov pistol was deemed obsolete and no longer capable of meeting the challenges of the new era. To develop a replacement, the USSR Ministry of Defense announced a competition, which led to the creation of an enhanced version of the 9x18mm cartridge, which was designated as +P+, as well as a modified version of the Makarov pistol adapted for this new ammunition. 
The updated pistol featured an improved chamber design, a wider grip, and a 12-round magazine. 
 Ammunition: 
 armor-piercing 9x18mm JSP-AP, 
 improved 9x18mm +P+.

A revolver-type grenade launcher developed by the Tula Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) in 1993. Its cylinder chambers are formed by six rifled, muzzle-loading barrels taken from GP-25 grenade launchers. 
It is highly valued by stalkers of the "Duty" faction for its effectiveness in clearing large areas of mutants.
 Ammunition:
 VOG-25 grenade,
 VOG-25P grenade.

A grenade launcher, model 1961, which remains in service with over 50 nations to this day. It is a smoothbore, single-shot, recoilless weapon with an open-ended barrel, designed to be fired from the shoulder. 
Within the Zone, it is an extremely rare sight, owing to its excessive weight and considerable size. It is occasionally employed for clearing out the lairs of pseudogiants or for hunting down military helicopters.
 Ammunition:
 OG-7B warhead.

The Kalashnikov light machine gun (RPK) was developed in the mid-1950s as a support weapon. 
Its primary advantages are its low weight (for an LMG) and a high capacity 75-round magazine (for an assault rifle). At the same time, this magazine capacity is quite small for an LMG, and its sustained automatic fire capability is limited due to a non-replaceable barrel and a closed-bolt firing mechanism. 
Consequently, it functions more as an intermediate option between an assault rifle and a proper LMG.
 Ammunition:
 standard 7.62x39mm.

The RPK-74 light machine gun was developed to replace the RPK as part of a small-arms system chambered for the 5.45mm low-impulse cartridge. 
Adopted for service in 1974, it suffers from the same design drawbacks as its predecessor: it still fires from a closed bolt, the barrel remains non-detachable, and the magazine capacity is insufficient for an LMG. At the same time, it retains key advantages, such as a relatively high magazine capacity (for an assault rifle) and a very low weight (for a light machine gun). 
Consequently, it functions more as an intermediate option between an assault rifle and a proper LMG.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.45x39mm FMJ,
 armor-piercing 5.45x39mm AP.

An export variant of the RPK-74 light machine gun, chambered for the 5.56x45mm cartridge and developed in 1994. It is popular in certain military conflicts beyond the Perimeter, but not within the Zone.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

A Swiss pistol developed back in the mid-1960s; it has remained the steadfast choice of the Swiss Army since 1978. 
Lightweight and as reliable as a Swiss watch, the SIG Sauer P220 is highly regarded worldwide. Its drawbacks include a limited magazine capacity, though this is partially offset by its powerful Colt cartridge.
 Ammunition:
 standard .45 ACP,
 improved .45 ACP Hydra-Shok.

The Swiss SIG SG 550 assault rifle was developed in the late 1970s as part of a competition for a new service rifle for the Swiss Army. The resulting design became the embodiment of Swiss quality — reliable, accurate, and easy to handle. 
Recognizing the merits of the new rifle, the Swiss Army officially adopted it in 1983. Since then, the SIG SG 550 and its variants have gained widespread popularity around the world.
 Ammunition:
 standard 5.56x45mm SS109,
 armor-piercing 5.56x45mm AP.

A smoothbore shotgun manufactured by the Italian firm Luigi Franchi, developed in the late 1970s as a versatile combat weapon for police and army assault units. 
SPAS-12 is characterized by high reliability, a high rate of fire, and operational flexibility, though these advantages come at the cost of significant weight and a bulky, cumbersome design.
 Ammunition:
 12x70Buckshot,
 12x76mm Slug,
 12x76mm Dart.

The Dragunov sniper rifle was adopted for service in 1963, following its victory in a competition held by the USSR Ministry of Defense. It is equipped with an integrated 8x-magnification sight. 
Owing to its high accuracy, exceptional reliability, and the use of a powerful sniper cartridge, it has proven its worth over the last half-century and remains in service with many nations worldwide. Its drawbacks include its large size, which is a characteristic typical of sniper rifles.
 Ammunition:
 standard 7.62x54R 7N1,
 armor-piercing 7.62x54R AP,
 improved 7.62x54R 7N14.

A shortened version of the Dragunov sniper rifle, developed by the Tula-based Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) back in the 1970s for the Soviet Airborne Forces. For a long time, it existed only as a series of prototypes, until it was revisited in the early 1990s. 
The use of a "bullpup" configuration significantly increased the rifle's compactness and maneuverability, making it an excellent choice for urban combat. 
It is equipped with an integrated 8x scope, as well as a specialized muzzle device that functions as both a flash suppressor and a muzzle brake.
 Ammunition:
 standard 7.62x54R 7N1,
 armor-piercing 7.62x54R AP,
 improved 7.62x54R 7N14.

A compact assault rifle chambered for a subsonic cartridge, developed in 1993 by the Tula Design Bureau (TsKIB SOO) commissioned by the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. Structurally based on the AKS-74U assault rifle, but has a number of differences from it due to conversion to a subsonic 9x39mm caliber cartridge. 
Despite its advantages, the "Tiss" did not gain much popularity and was withdrawn from service in favor of other weapons of the same caliber. Since then, small quantities of OTs-12s have occasionally surfaced on the black market.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x39mm PAB-9,
 armor-piercing 9x39mm SP-6,
 sniper 9x39mm SP-5.

A classic Soviet over-under shotgun, manufactured by the Tula Arms Plant (TOZ) from the mid-1960s all the way into the 1990s. TOZ-34 is particularly prized by hunters for its reliability and consistent performance across all of Russia’s diverse climatic zones. 
In total, more than 1.5 million TOZ-34s were produced; a significant number of these were rendered inoperable due to a simple failure to follow proper handling procedures during disassembly — a consequence of certain unique design features specific to this shotgun.
 Ammunition:
 12x70Buckshot,
 12x76mm Slug,
 12x76mm Dart.

The "Universal Self-Loading Pistol" (USP) is manufactured by the German firm Heckler & Koch. It was developed in the early 1990s for military and police use, with an emphasis on ease of handling and reliability. 
The "Compact" variant features a smaller frame, a shorter barrel, and a reduced magazine capacity.
 Ammunition:
 standard .45 ACP,
 improved .45 ACP Hydra-Shok.

A suppressed automatic rifle chambered for subsonic ammunition, developed by the Klimovsk-based CRI based on the VSS "Vintorez" as part of a unified family of special-purpose weapons. It is equipped with an extended 20-round magazine. 
When used with armor-piercing ammunition, it demonstrates high combat effectiveness against armored targets while maintaining a low signature, therefore minimizing the primary factors that could reveal the shooter's position.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x39mm PAB-9,
 armor-piercing 9x39mm SP-6,
 sniper 9x39mm SP-5.

A unique VSS "Vintorez" model featuring an upgraded 6x optical sight. 
Precision has been enhanced through expert fine-tuning, and the magazine has been replaced with a high-capacity 20-round version from the AS "Val."
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x39mm PAB-9,
 armor-piercing 9x39mm SP-6,
 sniper 9x39mm SP-5.

A suppressed sniper rifle chambered for subsonic ammunition, developed by the Klimovsk-based CRI for use in special operations. It features an integrated 4x optical sight. 
When used with specialized sniper ammunition, it offers an effective engagement range against lightly armored targets—accounting for the trajectory’s flatness—while maintaining a low signature in terms of key factors that might otherwise reveal the shooter's position.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x39mm PAB-9,
 armor-piercing 9x39mm SP-6,
 sniper 9x39mm SP-5.

An experimental VSS "Vintorez" model, modified by scientists from the "Magnet" group. 
The weapon's lethality has been increased by harnessing the anomalous properties of gravitational artifacts.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x39mm PAB-9,
 armor-piercing 9x39mm SP-6,
 sniper 9x39mm SP-5.

The German Walther P99 pistol was developed in the mid-1990s for law enforcement use and personal defense, and it gained fame as the sidearm featured in films about a certain British spy. 
It is an excellent, modern pistol, distinguished by its reliability, accuracy, compact design, and high-capacity magazine.
 Ammunition:
 standard 9x19mm Parabellum,
 improved 9x19mm JSP-AP.

In the second half of the 1980s the American firm Mossberg began production of the "Maverick 88" pump-action shotgun, designed for use in police and military special operations, as well as for self-defense, hunting, and sporting purposes. 
It is a highly affordable and reliable blued-steel firearm that successfully competes with more expensive models.
 Ammunition:
 12x70Buckshot,
 12x76mm Slug,
 12x76mm Dart.
